blocks.text: Psalm 89 moves from praise of Jehovah’s enduring faithfulness and covenant with David to an anguished protest that the anointed king’s crown has been cast down. Its closing blessing comes after, not instead of, the unanswered question “How long?” The psalm also stands at the end of Book III in the five-book arrangement of the Psalter, so this unresolved crisis forms part of that book’s closing movement.

Verses 19–37 recall a promise associated with David: an enduring house and throne, a father-and-son relationship, discipline when his descendants do wrong, and a commitment not to withdraw steadfast love. The later description of the king’s humiliation therefore creates the central tension of the psalm: it sets the remembered promise beside present rejection without supplying an easy resolution.

When the king is called God’s “first-born” and “the highest of the kings of the earth” in verse 27, “first-born” can be read in more than one way. Its possible implications for time, status, and inheritance are disputed; the verse’s own parallel description places particular emphasis on the king’s elevated rank.
